analysis.one_liner: Requires 401(k) plans to disclose all fees to employers and workers and to offer a low-cost index fund.
analysis.headline: The bill cleared the House Education and Labor Committee on a 25-19 vote in April 2008 but was never brought to the House floor before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would force companies that sell 401(k) services to tell employers, in writing, exactly what each service costs — itemized down to commissions, recordkeeping fees, and hidden payments for steering workers into certain funds. Workers would get an annual statement showing every fee deducted from their own account, compared against a simple index fund, and every 401(k) would have to offer at least one low-cost index option. It would also create a Labor Department council on retirement practices and give small employers help finding affordable plans.
analysis.who_benefits: The roughly tens of millions of workers who save in 401(k) plans. The bill does not cap fees, but it gives workers and their employers the numbers to see them: an itemized list of every charge a service provider expects to take, an annual statement showing each fee actually deducted from the worker's account, and a guaranteed low-cost index fund option to compare against. Small employers get Labor Department help choosing providers and investments. The Labor Department would also audit a sample of plans each year and report violators.

how_it_helps.text: Every contract for 401(k) services would require a written statement identifying who performs the services, describing each one, and itemizing the expected total annual cost — including sales commissions, start-up fees, investment management, recordkeeping, trustee and legal fees, termination charges, and hidden payments like 12b-1 fees and commissions under securities-law safe harbors.

Service providers would have to disclose conflicts of interest, including whether they push their own proprietary funds or get paid for having certain funds included in a plan's menu, and would have to explain when cheaper plan share prices differ from retail prices.

Participants would receive annual statements showing their contributions, earnings, and every fee charged against their account, itemized by type, with total fees shown both in dollars and as a percentage of assets, plus a comparison of their chosen investments to a nationally recognized market index.

Every plan letting workers choose investments would have to provide a plain-language 'fee menu' before each plan year, and at least one investment option would have to be a nationally recognized, market-based index fund.

The Labor Department would have to audit a representative sample of plans annually, notify securities regulators about service providers with patterns of noncompliance, publicize violator identities, and give small employers educational materials and help finding affordable investment options.

analysis.who_pays: The financial firms that earn money on 401(k) accounts: mutual fund companies collecting asset-based fees, insurers selling variable annuities inside plans, recordkeepers and administrators, and brokers and advisers earning commissions and revenue-sharing payments. All of these charges would have to be itemized and disclosed to the employers paying them and the workers bearing them, and the index-fund requirement would put a cheap benchmark next to higher-cost funds in every plan menu. Employers sponsoring plans would take on new compliance paperwork, though the bill directs the Labor Department to help them.
analysis.who_pays_short: Mutual fund, insurance, and 401(k) service firms

drawbacks.text: The bill imposes new contracting and disclosure paperwork on employers and plan administrators, and small businesses sponsoring plans would bear a share of that burden, though the bill directs the Labor Department to supply compliance materials and help for small employers.

Disclosure is not a fee cap: workers would see the charges but fees would still be legal, and where exact amounts are unknown the bill permits providers to give estimates, corrected later only if materially wrong — so a determined provider could still bury costs in reasonable-sounding estimates.

The requirement that every plan include an index fund and the detailed annual statement format would constrain plan design and add administrative cost, which critics of fee-disclosure rules argued can fall partly on participants through plan expenses.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core bargain is straightforward: paperwork and disclosure costs for employers and service providers, in exchange for workers finally seeing what they are being charged. Fees that look small — 1% of assets a year — compound into a large share of a lifetime's retirement savings, so the informational benefit is substantial. The bill's honest weaknesses are that it discloses rather than caps fees, relies on estimates that can be wrong until corrected, and adds real compliance work for small employers. On balance the benefits to savers outweigh the compliance costs, which the bill partially offsets with Labor Department assistance.

outcome.mechanism: It got a hearing, cleared the House Education and Labor Committee 25-19 in April 2008, and then sat without ever being brought to the House floor before the Congress ended in January 2009.

narrative.text: Rep. George Miller, the Democratic chair of the House Education and Labor Committee, introduced the bill on July 26, 2007, and it was referred to his committee.
The committee held hearings on October 4, 2007, referred it to a subcommittee on September 19, 2007, and on April 16, 2008 ordered it reported with amendments by a vote of 25-19.
No further action was ever recorded: the bill was never reported to the House, never debated, and never voted on before the 110th Congress ended on January 3, 2009.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The companies that earn 401(k) fees — mutual fund companies, insurers, recordkeepers, and brokers — are better off because the bill never became law, since the commissions, revenue-sharing payments, and asset-based charges it would have forced into the open continued without itemized disclosure to employers and workers.

for.name: Rep. George Miller
for.role: Chair, House Education and Labor Committee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and advanced it through his committee, including a hearing and an April 2008 markup where it was ordered reported with amendments.

against.name: 19 House Education and Labor Committee members
against.role: Committee members who voted against ordering the bill reported
against.what_they_did: Voted no at the April 16, 2008 markup, leaving the committee vote at 25-19.

against.name: House leadership
against.role: Speaker and House majority leadership, 110th Congress
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a House floor vote at any point in the 16 months after the committee approved it, through the end of the Congress.

against.name: Mutual fund and retirement plan service industries
against.role: Fund companies, insurers, and recordkeepers earning 401(k) fees
against.what_they_did: Opposed mandatory itemized fee disclosure and revenue-sharing transparency, which threatened a major, largely unseen revenue stream.

sides.party_line_note: The only recorded vote was the committee's 25-19 to advance the bill; the party affiliations of the individual yeas and nays are not in the record, though the bill had a Democratic sponsor and only Democratic cosponsors.

industries.note: Asset-based fees, expense ratios, and 12b-1 payments collected inside 401(k)s would have to be itemized for employers and shown to workers, and every plan would have to carry a low-fee index fund as a benchmark alternative. Since small annual fees compound into a large share of retirement savings, visibility is the direct threat to this revenue.

industries.industry: Insurance companies selling variable annuities in 401(k) plans
industries.note: The bill would require disclosing mortality and expense charges, surrender and termination penalties, and employer stock fees line by line on annual participant statements — charges that are currently hard for participants to see.

Revenue-sharing arrangements, 'free' services recouped through participant account charges, commissions, and conflicts of interest would all have to be disclosed in writing before contracts are signed and updated annually, with violators publicly identified by the Labor Department.

Sponsors would face new contracting, disclosure, and annual-statement duties, but the bill directs the Labor Department to provide compliance materials and help finding affordable options, and employers gain the same cost visibility their workers do.
